title: password_policy.v2
description: The rule an authentication system applies to the passwords of the identities it governs. v1 modelled AWS IAM's answer sheet — eight required fields, four of them character-class booleans — which no other vendor can fill: Google rates a password STRONG or WEAK and says in its own documentation that strength is entropy plus breach screening, explicitly NOT a character-class rule; Entra fixes length and complexity as platform constants and exposes neither as a tenant setting. v2 makes three changes and nothing else. (1) Complexity is a discriminated union: complexity_model names the KIND of answer the source has (per_class | strength_enum | fixed | none) and the fields carrying that answer are required only for their own kind, so a source states what it observed instead of being squeezed into four booleans it cannot fill. (2) Reuse is answered as a boolean (reuse_prevented) with the depth as an optional refinement, because some vendors prevent reuse without disclosing how far back. (3) Everything a platform may not let a tenant configure is optional, so absence is expressible. Absence has exactly one meaning: THIS SOURCE DID NOT OBSERVE A VALUE. It is never a zero, never a floor, and never the vendor's documented default — a default is a value the tenant could have changed, so reading one out of documentation says nothing about this tenant and must not be signed into evidence. Where the platform forbids configuration altogether, say so in not_configurable rather than inventing the constant. An account/tenant may be governed by one policy (AWS) or several (Okta group-assigned, Google per-OU, Entra per-domain); a source emits one record per policy in force and consuming policies quantify over all of them, which reads as "every password policy in force meets the bar".

id.description: Unique within the emitting source — the vendor's policy identifier where there is one, else a stable identifier for the singleton (AWS emits "account"). Violations are deduplicated by it, so two policies must never share one.

name.description: Human-readable policy name as the administrator sees it in the vendor console. Optional: AWS's account password policy has no name. Present only to let an auditor find the policy being described; no shipped clause reads it.

provider.description: Short name of the system enforcing the policy: aws, okta, google_workspace, entra. Required — it is the one field no plausible source can fail to know about itself.

scope.description: The kind of population this policy governs. Required: a source had to ask the API for a policy somehow, so it always knows what the answer applies to. account = every identity in the account/tenant/org (AWS's account policy, Okta's system default policy); domain = one verified domain of a tenant (Entra); org_unit = one branch of a directory tree (Google Workspace); group = the members of one or more groups (Okta group-assigned, AD fine-grained); user = one identity. The field exists so several records are not read as interchangeable: it says what each one covers.

precedence.description: Rank among policies that COMPETE for the same identity, 1 = evaluated first and wins. The plugin normalizes the vendor's ordering into this rank (Okta's priority is already 1 = highest; Google's sortOrder is the reverse and must be inverted). Optional, and its absence carries meaning: omit it when the emitted policies do not compete — one per domain, or a singleton — so that presence says "these are alternatives, one of which governs a given identity" and absence says "each governs its own disjoint population". No shipped clause reads it; a future effective-policy reduction has nothing to work from without it.

min_length.description: Minimum password length the policy requires. 0 means an observed absence of any minimum — the platform has a policy and it imposes no floor (AWS with no account password policy configured). Omit the field entirely when the value was not observed: a platform that does not expose it (Entra, where 8 is a Microsoft constant) or a vendor that returned null. Emitting 0 for an unread value would sign "this org has no minimum" into evidence when what we know is that nothing was reported.

max_age_days.description: Maximum password age in days before forced rotation. 0 means an observed "no expiry" (which NIST 800-63B and several vendors now treat as correct when rotation is event-driven), not "unknown". Omit when not observed.

reuse_prevented.description: Whether the policy prevents a previous password from being set again. This is the canonical reuse answer because it is the only one every vendor can give: AWS and Okta disclose a history depth, Google exposes allowReuse as a bare boolean and documents no depth at all. Omit when not observed.

reuse_prevention_count.description: How many previous passwords the policy remembers, when the vendor discloses the depth. A refinement of reuse_prevented, never a substitute: a source that knows the depth emits both (the schema requires it), and a source that knows only that reuse is blocked emits reuse_prevented alone rather than guessing a number. 0 means an observed "no history kept".

complexity_model.description: Which KIND of strength answer this source has, and therefore which fields below carry it. per_class = the policy is stated as character-class requirements (AWS, Okta, AD) → the four requires_* booleans. strength_enum = the platform rates candidate passwords on its own scale and the policy names the minimum acceptable rating (Google's allowedStrength) → password_strength. fixed = the platform enforces a strength requirement the tenant cannot configure or weaken (Entra's character-class rule for cloud-only accounts) → complexity_description. none = an observed absence of any strength requirement (an AWS account with no password policy at all). Omit the field when the source cannot tell — which is not the same as none, and is why none is spelled out rather than implied by absence. fixed is the one value derived from a platform's documented behaviour rather than a tenant read, and it is legitimate only for a rule the tenant CANNOT change: a constant is true of every tenant by construction, whereas a default is a value the tenant may have overridden, so a default must never be emitted here.

requires_uppercase.description: Password must contain at least one uppercase letter. Required when complexity_model is per_class, meaningless otherwise.

requires_lowercase.description: Password must contain at least one lowercase letter. Required when complexity_model is per_class, meaningless otherwise.

requires_numbers.description: Password must contain at least one digit. Required when complexity_model is per_class, meaningless otherwise.

requires_symbols.description: Password must contain at least one symbol. Required when complexity_model is per_class, meaningless otherwise.

password_strength.description: The minimum strength rating the platform will accept, on the platform's own scale. Required when complexity_model is strength_enum. Deliberately not translated into the four booleans: Google states that a strong password "doesn't need to have a specific number of characters of a specific type", so mapping strong to all-four-true would be a claim the vendor itself disclaims.

complexity_description.description: What the platform-enforced requirement actually is, in one line, for the auditor reading the envelope (e.g. "three of four character classes, enforced by the platform for cloud-only accounts and not tenant-configurable"). Required when complexity_model is fixed, because "fixed" on its own tells an auditor nothing about what is fixed. No clause reads it.

not_configurable.description: Attributes the platform exposes no tenant setting for, so their absence above is structural rather than unread. This is the difference between "Entra does not let you set a minimum length" and "we did not read one", and it is a statement about the platform's API surface — not a measurement dressed up as one, which is why the VALUE still stays absent. Omit the field when every attribute is configurable.

mfa_required.description: MFA is required at sign-on. An IdP-level sign-on concept rather than a password attribute, carried here for sources whose password policy object also states it; omit otherwise.
